answer_text:
Let  
\[
\theta=\alpha+\beta.
\]

Since \(\alpha\) is acute and \(\sin\alpha=\frac57\),

\[
\cos\alpha=\sqrt{1-\sin^2\alpha}
=\sqrt{1-\frac{25}{49}}
=\sqrt{\frac{24}{49}}
=\frac{2\sqrt6}{7}.
\]

Also,

\[
\cos(\alpha+\beta)=\frac{11}{14}.
\]

Taking the first-quadrant value for \(\sin(\alpha+\beta)\),

\[
\sin(\alpha+\beta)
=\sqrt{1-\cos^2(\alpha+\beta)}
=\sqrt{1-\frac{121}{196}}
=\sqrt{\frac{75}{196}}
=\frac{5\sqrt3}{14}.
\]

Now use
\[
\cos\beta=\cos\bigl((\alpha+\beta)-\alpha\bigr)

\]

Substitute:

\[
\cos\beta
=
\left(\frac{11}{14}\right)\left(\frac{2\sqrt6}{7}\right)

\[
\cos\beta
=
\frac{22\sqrt6}{98}+\frac{25\sqrt3}{98}
=

\]

Thus the formal value is

\[
\boxed{\frac{22\sqrt6+25\sqrt3}{98}}.
\]

Note: Strictly speaking, the stated conditions are inconsistent. Since \(\alpha\) is acute, \(\alpha\approx 45.6^\circ\), but \(\alpha+\beta\) would have to satisfy \(\cos(\alpha+\beta)=11/14\), giving \(\alpha+\beta\approx 38.2^\circ\), which would make \(\beta<0\), not acute. So no such acute \(\alpha,\beta\) actually exist; the boxed value is the algebraic value obtained from the given equations.
